queries.hook: I feel jealous of someone close to me. Inside, something doesn't sit right and I can't name it, and I don't know how to carry it.
queries.diagnose: Comparison and envy burn at another's success; measuring your life against theirs steals the contentment in your own.
queries.steady: Your own path, walked imperfectly, is better than another's walked well; what is yours is enough to begin with.
queries.act: Walk your own path, even imperfectly, rather than someone else's well; be grateful for what is yours and rejoice in others' good.
queries.story: A story of a seeker whose mind will not settle, facing measuring yourself against others.

hook.speaker: Kausalya
hook.setting: After lashing out at Dasharatha over Ram's exile, Kausalya apologises.
hook.sanskrit: जानामि धर्मे धर्मज्ञ त्वां जाने सत्यवादिनम्। पुत्रशोकार्तया तत्तु मया किमपि भाषितम्॥
hook.line: I know you are honest. I said those words out of my own pain.
hook.translation: I know what is right, righteous one, and I know you are truthful. It was in my anguish over my son that I said what I said.
hook.why: Grief makes us wound those we love; apologising quickly heals more than being right.

prasang.title: Kausalya's reproach and apology
prasang.summary: In her grief Kausalya lashes out at her husband for exiling their son. When he folds his hands and asks her forgiveness, she is horrified, apologises, and explains that grief made her speak.
prasang.story_hook: She said the words; then she saw her husband fold his hands to her.
prasang.lesson: Grief makes us wound those we love; apologising quickly heals more than being right.

alternates.speaker: Bharat
alternates.setting: After fourteen years, Hanuman brings Bharat the news that Ram is coming; Bharat has one question.
alternates.sanskrit: तब हनुमंत नाइ पद माथा। कहे सकल रघुपति गुन गाथा॥ कहु कपि कबहुँ कृपाल गोसाईं। सुमिरहिं मोहि दास की नाईं ॥
alternates.line: Tell me: does he ever think of me?
alternates.translation: Then Hanuman bowed at his feet and told all of Raghupati's virtues. 'Tell me, Hanuman: does the kind master ever remember me, as one remembers a servant?'

alternates.speaker: Manu
alternates.setting: Manu, offered any boon after years of austerity, hesitates to ask for what he truly wants.
alternates.sanskrit: जथा दरिद्र बिबुधतरु पाई। बहु संपति मागत सकुचाई॥ तासु प्रभाउ जान नहिं सोई। तथा हृदयँ मम संसय होई ॥
alternates.line: Like a poor man before the wishing tree, we hesitate to ask for what we really want.
alternates.translation: Like a poor man who finds the wish-fulfilling tree and still hesitates to ask for much, not knowing its power, so doubt rises in my heart.
alternates.why: It is not too late to turn towards what matters, but it takes courage to ask for it.

prasang.title: Manu and Shatarupa ask late in life
prasang.summary: King Manu and Queen Shatarupa realise in old age that a whole life has passed without what mattered most to them. They hand over the kingdom, go to the forest and practise austerity for years. When Vishnu offers a boon, Manu hesitates like a poor man before the wishing tree, then asks for a son like God himself.
prasang.story_hook: The king had ruled well for a lifetime, and one morning he realised he had missed the point.
prasang.lesson: It is not too late to turn towards what matters, but it takes courage to ask for it.

verse.speaker: A brahmin (retold by Bhishma)
verse.setting: The brahmin explains to King Senajit why loss hurts so much.
verse.sanskrit: किंचिदेव ममत्वेन यदा भवति कल्पितम् / तदेव परितापाय नाशे संपद्यते तदा
verse.line: Whatever you start calling 'mine' becomes a source of pain the day you lose it.
verse.translation: Whatever a person begins to think of as 'mine', that very thing becomes a source of anguish when it is lost.
verse.why: No one suffers forever. Meet what comes with an undefeated heart.

prasang.title: King Senajit and the brahmin's consolation
prasang.summary: King Senajit is crushed by his son's death. A brahmin comforts him: everyone suffers, no sorrow lasts forever, effort beats idleness, and whatever we call 'mine' becomes a source of pain.
prasang.lesson: No one suffers forever. Meet what comes with an undefeated heart.

verse.for_you: You said you cried after congratulating her, and that feeling does not sit right. The hurt comes from calling her success and your bond yours, then feeling the loss of that bond. Let the congratulations stand without claiming it as yours.
verse.try_today: Notice when you call a friendship yours, and let the moment pass without holding it.
verse.scene_line: You sit with your friend's news and your own grief, and the word mine holds them both.

why: The night she stopped waiting (Mahabharata, Shanti Parva 173-174 (Gita Press))
Explains the size of the pain without denying it

verse.speaker: Ram
verse.setting: Ram to Bharat, who blames himself for the exile and their father's death.
verse.sanskrit: तात जायँ जियँ करहु गलानी। ईस अधीन जीव गति जानी॥ तीनि काल तिभुअन मत मोरें। पुन्यसिलोक तात तर तोरें ॥
verse.line: You torment yourself with shame for nothing. In my eyes you stand above them all.
verse.translation: Brother, you torment your heart with shame for nothing; know that a soul's course is in God's hands. In my view, all the virtuous of past, present and future, in all three worlds, stand below you.
verse.why: In family conflict, let each speak; name love plainly; lift needless shame.

matched.label: I feel ashamed of who I am

prasang.title: The family council at Chitrakoot
prasang.summary: Vasishtha asks how Ram can be brought home, noting that grieving people cannot judge well. Bharat recalls a brother who never broke his heart and let him win at games, and blames himself. Ram tells him his shame is needless, that love and hostility cannot be hidden, and asks him to say freely what he wants.
prasang.lesson: In family conflict, let each speak; name love plainly; lift needless shame.

verse.for_you: You congratulated her and then went and cried in the bathroom. Your heart is heavy with a grief that does not sit right. Know that your course is in hands far larger than your own.
verse.try_today: Notice one moment today where your heart feels lighter than it did yesterday.
verse.scene_line: You stand in the bathroom, crying, while your friend celebrates her victory in another room.

why: The texts send a voice that lifts the shame: 'you torment yourself for nothing'.
the very person he believes he wronged tells him the shame is for nothing

verse.speaker: Lakshman
verse.setting: Sita has been taken; Lakshman, the younger brother, gently tries to bring Ram back to himself.
verse.sanskrit: बुद्धिश्च ते महाप्राज्ञ देवैरपि दुरन्वया। शोकेनाभिप्रसुप्तं ते ज्ञानं सम्बोधयाम्यहम्॥
verse.line: Your wisdom isn't gone. Grief has only put it to sleep for a while.
verse.translation: Your understanding, wise one, is beyond even the gods' reckoning. Grief has only put your wisdom to sleep, and I am here to wake it.
verse.for_you: You are not wrong to feel this way. Your understanding is still there, only resting for now.
verse.try_today: Notice when your wisdom shows up, even for a moment, and let it rest there.
verse.scene_line: You sit beside your friend's good news, and grief has put your own wisdom to sleep.

why: Feelings come and go, bear them; your wisdom is asleep, not gone (Lakshmana to Rama).
grief is treated as a sleep over wisdom, not its loss

verse.speaker: Vidura
verse.setting: Vidura counsels the sleepless King Dhritarashtra the night before the peace talks.
verse.sanskrit: किं नु मे स्यादिदं कृत्वा किं नु मे स्यादकुर्वतः / इति कर्माणि सञ्चिन्त्य कुर्याद्वा पुरुषो न वा
verse.line: Before acting, ask two questions: what happens if I do this, and what happens if I don't?
verse.translation: 'What will happen to me if I do this? What will happen if I don't?' Thinking actions through this way, a person should then act, or not act.
verse.why: Think before acting; if you did it right and it failed, don't sink. Guard your tongue.

prasang.title: Vidura Niti: careful action and wounding words
prasang.summary: Vidura continues through the night: weigh an action before you start it, don't sink when honest effort fails, and remember that words wound deeper than axes.
prasang.lesson: Think before acting; if you did it right and it failed, don't sink. Guard your tongue.

verse.for_you: You congratulated your friend, and then you cried in the bathroom. You are not sure which feeling to trust. Ask yourself what happens if you stay in that grief, and what happens if you let yourself be happy for her.
verse.try_today: Before you do the next small thing, ask what happens if you do it and if you do not.

why: Weigh the two duties; ask what happens if I do and if I do not.

verse.speaker: Teacher
verse.setting: The teacher's advice for when the rules run out.
verse.sanskrit: अथ यदि ते कर्मविचिकित्सा वा वृत्तविचिकित्सा वा स्यात् ॥ ये तत्र ब्राह्मणाः संमर्शिनः । युक्ता आयुक्ताः । अलूक्षा धर्मकामाः स्युः । यथा ते तत्र वर्तेरन् । तथा तत्र वर्तेथाः । अथाभ्याख्यातेषु । ये तत्र ब्राह्मणाः संमर्शिनः । युक्ता आयुक्ताः । अलूक्षा धर्मकामाः स्युः । यथा ते तेषु वर्तेरन् । तथा तेषु वर्तेथाः । एष आदेशः । एष उपदेशः ।
verse.line: When unsure what to do, ask how thoughtful, gentle, fair-minded people would act, and do that.
verse.translation: Now, if you are ever unsure about an action or about conduct, look to the thoughtful people there: devoted, independent, not harsh, lovers of what is right. As they would act, so should you act. And towards people under accusation, act as such people would. This is the instruction, this is the teaching.
verse.why: Truth, right action, gratitude and graceful giving: a whole life in one speech.

prasang.title: The graduation address
prasang.summary: As a student finishes his studies and leaves to start family life, the teacher gives him parting instructions: speak truth, do right, keep learning, honour mother, father, teacher and guest, give with grace. He even tells the student to copy only the teachers' good conduct, and when in doubt to act as thoughtful, gentle people would.
prasang.lesson: Truth, right action, gratitude and graceful giving: a whole life in one speech.

verse.for_you: You hate that your friend's good news made you cry in the bathroom. You do not need to be glad for her. You only need to act as the gentle, fair-minded people you already know would act, and that is enough for today.
verse.try_today: Notice one person nearby today who acts with quiet fairness, and let their conduct guide your next small choice.
verse.scene_line: You stand in the bathroom, and the teacher asks you to act as the thoughtful people there would act.

why: judgement is borrowed from people who are thoughtful, unforced and not harsh

story.title: Tulsidas, the boy who begged for scraps
story.story_hook: The poet of the Ramcharitmanas began life as an unwanted child begging for scraps in the lanes.
story.summary: Across his later works Tulsidas tells his own story: left by his parents at birth, he wandered door to door for scraps, no job, no trade, no skill, ignored by everyone. Good people told him not to worry; Hanuman raised him like a child; Ram's name, he says, turned a thorny babul into a mango tree. Even when he went astray, he was taken back.
story.lesson: Where you start is not where you end; you can be taken in from nothing.
story.hook_title: Tulsidas began life as an unwanted child begging for scraps
story.teaser: Tulsidas began life as an unwanted child begging for scraps
story.for_you: Your friend's good news arrived like a door closing on a room you wanted to stay in. That ache is real. A single honest cry, even in a bathroom stall, is enough to be heard.
